extracted.intended_audience: practical metallurgists, assayers, miners and early modern alchemists (readers seeking hands-on recipes and standards for processing and evaluating metals and pigments)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and theoretical rules for identifying, extracting, purifying, and using metals and metal-derived pigments (recipes, procedures, diagnostic properties, and locations for ore). Contains hands-on recipes (distillations, calcinings) and evaluative criteria (density, tenacity, color, fire-resistance, provenance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Production of red cinnabar-like pigment (cinnabaris)
rubrics_metrics.description: Heat sulphur in an olla and add twice the quantity of argentum vivum (quicksilver/mercury); mix continuously under heat and distill until no species of argentum vivum appears and a red smoke emerges. The product is used for writing and painting as a red color, imitating native cinnabar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep continuous mixing under sustained fire; observe until red fumes ('ruber fumus') appear and then finish distillation. The resulting red is fit for ink and pigments; if any remnants persist, regrind in a mortar with acetic acid and reheat/refine. The recipe emphasizes repeated distillation and purification to obtain a bright red suitable for painting ('ad scribendum ac pingendum rubro colore').

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublimation/distillation to obtain 'argentum fublimatur' and precipitated red silver (precipitatum)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sublimate (fublimatur) argentum (mercurial/metallic residues) by combining with substances such as alumen and calchantum in portions and distilling in glass vessels until smoke reddens and nothing else remains; collect the condensed argentum vivum from cooled glassware.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use vitreous (glass) vases for distillation, apply repeated heating until the glass reddens and smoke appears. Collect residues carefully after cooling; if any remains uncoagulated, triturate with vinegar in a mortar and reheat. This method yields 'argentum coctum rubrum' often termed 'precipitatum'. Follow multiple cycles of calcination and distillation to purify fully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation of pforicum (pyrophoric product)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pforicum is made from two parts of calx (calchantum) and one part cadmia or from silver scum (spuma argenti); mix, add sharp white vinegar, grind, then bury/season in warm earth for ~40 days (canicular/equine heat).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After trituration with vinegar, bury the mixture in warmed earth or ashes for the given period (forty days) to complete transformation. This long, mild maturation is required rather than only fire treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smaltum (glass-based pigment) production and use
rubrics_metrics.description: Smaltum is a type of glass product used to fill cavities with golden hues or varied coloured beauty; it is obtained by roasting (with charcoal) until reddened; accepts varied colors and is used for decorative inlay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Roast in new fired crucibles with charcoal until it reddens; it accepts a wide range of colors and shines when made well. Consider mixing smaltum with other vitreous colors for desired effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collecting and treating recrementum (residual metal scoria / spuma)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recrementum is the residue/foam that remains when metals are calcined; it retains some metallic virtues and should be collected and sometimes re-calcined to recover metal qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During calcination, collect the 'spuma' (foam) and process it further (re-cook) to extract retained metallic virtues. If it will not melt with the liquated metal, regard it as a stone-like residue and treat accordingly (grind, roast, and re-calcine).

rubrics_metrics.name: Production and classification of cadmia, pompholix, and spodon (calcinates used medicinally)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cadmia arises natively or when metal is calcined and adheres like a grape (botrus); pompholix is a bubble-like product obtained during calcination; spodon is a purer form often found in towns. All are used principally in ocular medicines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer cadmia from certain ores (pyrites giving candida cadmia) for quality; pompholix and spodon may substitute for each other in ocular remedies. Distinguish the varieties by color and mode of formation (surface of furnaces vs. smoke deposits) and choose the most suitable (candida) for medical uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal and gathering of ferrugo (iron rust) and its processing
rubrics_metrics.description: To remove and collect ferrugo (rust) from vessels, put the rusted vessel into strong vinegar in a shallow pit for days, removing scale; repeat operations to gather ferrugo which can be dried and used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a warm vinegar bath in a clay-lined receptacle; after several days, scrape off rust and collect. Iteration improves yield. Note ferrugo both tightens and dries surfaces and can erode if aggressive; manage exposure time to avoid over-erosion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making vermicular (vermicularis) coatings (vermicular pigment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mix white alum and parts of vinegar and certain aluminous components in specified proportions, place perforated thin silver leaves in the vessel, agitate with a pestle over sun-exposure and repeated cycles (dozens of days) to produce vermicular (worm-like) colored flakes akin to honey in thickness and splendid color.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infuse three pounds of distilled sharp vinegar prepared with ammoniac-like additions, suspend perforated silver discs on a rod above but not touching the vinegar, expose to warmer equine heat for multiple cycles (around 20–40 days per cycle), then collect and wash off the blue/verdigris-like deposit. Repeat as necessary to intensify color.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production of ceruleum (blue pigment) by vinegar-induced surface coloration
rubrics_metrics.description: In a vessel of very sharp vinegar with a portion of ammoniac dissolved, hang thin perforated silver plates on a suspended rod, warm for ~20 days; the silver when removed shows cerulean (blue) coloration which can be scraped and refined into a pigment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suspend the plates so they do not touch the vinegar, keep the vessel warm but not touching the fire, withdraw after ~20 days, and if further intensity is needed, repeat the cycle. After collection, wash and dry the powder in the sun and further process as with other pigments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation of cerussa (white lead) by acetic vapor fermentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Produce ceruffam (white lead) by placing thin sheets/bracteae of lead into sharp vinegar, cover with yeasts (fermenta of bread), bury/keep in warm conditions (~25 days), and collect the calcinated white lead formed on the metal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternative higher-quality cerussas come from specific regions (Hispania). For careful production: distill and dry residues, sieve and sun-dry the resulting powder. Multiple cycles (remove after first 10 days, repeat) yield finer white lead. Urine distillation is an alternate method for some variants ('Ranum').

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiation and production of argentum spuma and plumbago by calcination
rubrics_metrics.description: Argenti spuma (silver foam) and plumbago arise when silver and lead are combined and calcined; the spuming/foam corresponds to portions of metal and impurities and may proceed to plumbago (lead-derived powder) through heating and reduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When silver is melted with lead and exposed to fire, the foamy residues (spuma) separate; process these by grinding and calcining to convert to plumbago or litharge-like products. Note color differences (plumbago outer similarity, inner parts greyish) and adapt further refinement accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition and manufacture of purpurina (purple pigment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Purpurina consists chiefly of white lead and argentum vivum in equal portions, with additions of ammoniac and sulphur. Mix in a glass vessel, distil; the residue left is purpurina.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the white lead is very fine (thin leaves/filings). Mix thoroughly in a vitreous vessel and distil; what remains at the bottom after distillation is the purpurina. Control proportions (ratios given as equal or fractional parts) and repeat distillations to intensify color.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory: metals composed of two principal parts (thin/igneous and earthy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every metallic material made by art consists of two parts: one thin and igneous (volatile/fiery) that gives color and light, and another earthy/terrestrial part that fixes and makes the substance hard. The composite behavior depends on their proportion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this two-part model to predict metal behavior: more igneous/thin part yields tenacity, color brilliance, and susceptibility to fire; more earthy part yields fixation and hardness. This guides both processing and intended use (jewelry vs. pigments vs. adulteration).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical uses of metallic artifices (three main uses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Art-made metallics serve three principal purposes: for ornamentation of the human body (jewelry), for painting (pigments, glasses), and for adulterating metals and gems; a fourth possible use is medicinal/poisonous applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose processing routes and recipes depending on intended use: produce thin, brilliant metals for gilding or durable fixed substances for tools, and specific calcinates or pigments for painting. Recognize that some recipes that suit pigments may be harmful if used on the body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of natural metals and planetary correspondences
rubrics_metrics.description: Lists natural metals (seven principal): aurum (gold), argentum (silver), electrum, aes (copper), stannum (tin), cyprium (brass/copper alloy), plumbum (lead), ferrum (iron) with correspondences (Sun–gold, Moon–silver, Mercury–electrum, Mars–iron, Saturn–lead, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these classifications to reason about properties (e.g., gold is most perfect and lustrous, iron/dense/hard) and regional expectations (some metals more common in eastern vs. western regions). This also informs expectations about behavior under heat and corrosion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locating and extracting gold (prospecting guidelines)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gold is found in several ways: in sandy alluvia of rivers (alluvial gold), in native spots on mountain summits, within mixed metals in ores, among silver-bearing veins, and in specific named localities (e.g., Bohemia, Liguria, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect and pan river sands and alluvium, avoid excessive trenching for minimal yield, prefer collecting from river mouths and lake bottoms where gold accumulates, and treat extracted gravels rather than deep excavation unless abundance justifies the labor. Washing and agitation concentrate gold; do not expect huge returns everywhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic properties to evaluate metals (color, tenacity, density, fire-resistance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Metals are evaluated by characteristics: color (nitorem/shine), tenacity (ductility/malleability), density (weight per volume), resistance to fire (whether the metal is consumed or altered by heating), smell/odour when heated, and behavior on beating into leaves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gold: most perfect, very thin and malleable, resists fire (does not consume), has pleasant odor under heat; silver: next most perfect but less resistant to fire; iron/lead less lustrous and more impure. Use comparative tests (heating, beating, dissolving) to assess rank and purity. Larger sample mass reduces assay error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules and procedures for separating/purifying gold from silver (aqua separationis and gravimetric separation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate gold by liquation/separation in 'aqua separationis' so that denser gold descends to the bottom; collect and purify. Other methods include adding sulphur or stibium in small proportions to cause gold to descend, or repeated layerings of powdered materials and heating to extinguish impurities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit density differences (gold heavier than silver) and differing behaviours to fire/acid. Liquate the mass and collect lower portion; if necessary, mix with sulphur or stibium in prescribed fractions to help gold settle. Repeat heating and washing cycles to improve purity. Note: argentum vivum (mercury) may be used to amalgamate and help separate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on transmutation of metals (theoretical constraints)
rubrics_metrics.description: Chymists (alchemists) may change outward colors and weight and can perform partial exchanges between similar metals, but cannot change the inner subtlety and firmness of metals entirely; true transmutation (e.g., base metal to perfect gold) is doubtful or requires special conditions and often impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be skeptical of claims of full transmutation. Expect possible changes in color and apparent weight by alloying and refining, especially between metals of similar density and tenacity (e.g., iron ↔ copper), but not wholesale change of species. Use experimental evidence (persistence under fire, density, tenacity) to test claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling rule for metallurgical experiments (mass reduces assay error)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is safe to test a metal when the sample is large; small samples introduce risk of error. Larger masses reduce the danger of mistaken results when trying fusion, separation, or transformations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid conducting experimental separation or transmutation on minute quantities of precious metal; ensure a reasonably large mass (examples given: measures in pounds, ounces, scruples) to reduce relative error and misleading observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement of tenuity and malleability as a diagnostic metric (beating gold leaf)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tenuity (thinness) is an indicator of purity: gold can be beaten to extremely thin leaves and cover very large areas. Gold's tenuity compared with other metals (e.g., mixing gold grain with iron alters properties) serves as a measure of its perfection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test by hammering/bractea production; record the ratio of gold to other metals by weight (e.g., grains and pounds) to gauge how many times thinner than other metals the gold is. Use standard units (uncia, scrupulum, grains) cited in text when assessing tenuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency/translucency (perpicuum) criteria for stones and metals
rubrics_metrics.description: A substance is transparent ('perpicuum') if light and luminance can pass through; liquids, airs, and some thin metals admit light while earth does not. Very thin metallic leaves or certain stones may become translucent if thin enough, but terra (earth) cannot become truly transparent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test transparency by thinness and by mixing with oils: oil with a transparent material may render it opaque. Use thinning (hammering, grinding to powder, mixing with clear binders) and avoid earthy admixtures that block light. This guides production of glass and gem-like artifices.
